issues.legal_issue: A party’s failure to testify on their own behalf and submit to cross-examination may support an adverse inference against that party.
material_facts: The defendant who disputed the sale did not enter the witness box or testify under oath to the facts pleaded in his defence.
The disputed transaction and any payment under it had not occurred in that defendant’s presence, and he had no personal knowledge of its terms.
The defendant avoided cross-examination while the vendor admitted the plaintiff’s claim and testified to the sale.
issues.conclusion: An adverse presumption arose against the defendant who withheld his testimony, supporting rejection of his claim that the sale was fictitious.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, the court may draw an adverse inference when a party does not testify to their own case and submit to cross-examination. The Court relied on Sardar Gurbakhsh Singh v. Gurdial Singh, Kirpa Singh v. Ajaipal Singh, Martand Pandharinath Chaudhari v. Radhabai Krishnarao Deshmukh, Gulla Kharagjit Carpenter v. Narsingh Nandkishore Rawat, Arjun Singh v. Virender Nath, and Bhagwan Dass v. Bhishan Chand.

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.party_did_not_testify: A party did not enter the witness box to give their own evidence on the case they pleaded.
predicates.party_did_not_submit_to_cross_examinatio: The party did not make themselves available for cross-examination by the opposing side.

issues.definition: When a party in a civil suit does not testify to their case or submit to cross-examination, an adverse inference may be drawn against that party.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant who is not a party to a transfer may plead and prove that the transfer deed is fictitious, sham, or collusive.
material_facts: The defendant challenging the sale was not a party to the sale between the vendor and the purchaser.
The defendant alleged that the sale deed was fictitious because the full consideration had not been paid.
The Court distinguished a deed intended to effect a genuine transfer from one never intended to operate as a transfer of title.
issues.conclusion: A defendant may raise a legitimate defence that a deed is void, fictitious, or collusive, including when the defendant is a stranger to that deed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to apply the broad formulation in Lal Achal Ram v. Raja Kazim Hussain Khan so as to prevent every challenge by a stranger. It approved the approach in Kamini Kumar Deb v. Durga Charan Nag, Saradindu Mukherjee v. S.M. Kunja Katnini Roy, Jugal Kishore Tiwari v. Umesh Chandra Tiwari, and Sanatan Mohapatra v. Hakim Mohammad Kazim Mohammad: a defendant may raise a legitimate plea that a deed was void, fictitious, or collusive, and whether the deed was genuine depends on the pleadings, nature of the suit and deed, evidence, and surrounding circumstances.

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.challenger_is_not_party_to_deed: The defendant challenging the deed was not a party to the transaction recorded in it.
predicates.deed_is_alleged_to_be_sham_or_collusive: The defendant alleged that the deed was not intended to effect a genuine transfer of title.

issues.definition: A defendant in a civil suit who was not a party to a deed may challenge it as sham or collusive when alleging that it was not intended to effect a genuine transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A stranger to a genuine sale deed cannot dispute the payment or adequacy of its consideration when the challenge concerns only consideration.
material_facts: The defendant challenging the sale deed was not a party to the transaction between the vendor and the purchaser and had no personal knowledge of its terms or payment.
The vendor admitted the claim based on the sale deed, did not challenge it, and testified that he executed the deed and received the consideration.
The lower courts found the registered sale deed genuine, and the challenge at issue concerned whether the full consideration had been paid.
issues.conclusion: The defendant could not invalidate the sale deed merely by disputing the payment or adequacy of consideration.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle in Lal Achal Ram v. Raja Kazim Hussain Khan that a stranger to a genuine sale deed cannot dispute payment or adequacy of consideration, while distinguishing a deed alleged to be fictitious or collusive. The vendor, as executant, could have disputed consideration, but admitted the sale and its consideration.

rule.if: civil_suit and challenger_is_stranger_to_transfer and deed_was_intended_to_transfer_title and challenge_is_only_about_consideration

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.challenger_is_stranger_to_transfer: The defendant challenging the transaction was not a party to it.
predicates.deed_was_intended_to_transfer_title: The deed was intended by its parties to effect a genuine transfer of title.
predicates.challenge_is_only_about_consideration: The challenge concerned whether the consideration was paid or was adequate, rather than whether the deed was fictitious or collusive.

issues.definition: A defendant who was a stranger to a genuine transfer cannot defeat it by challenging only the payment or adequacy of its consideration.

issues.legal_issue: A party may bring a witness to give evidence without a summons, and the witness’s examination is not invalid merely because the witness was omitted from the list of witnesses.
material_facts: In the civil suit, the plaintiff brought the vendor to testify without obtaining a summons.
The vendor’s name was not included in the plaintiff’s list of witnesses.
The court examined the vendor, who admitted executing the sale deed and receiving the consideration.
issues.conclusion: The vendor was properly examined, and his testimony was not open to criticism merely because he was not listed or summoned through the court.
issues.legal_principle: Order XVI Rules 1 and 1A of the Code of Civil Procedure permit a party to bring a witness without applying for a summons; Rule 1A and Rule 1(3) address different situations. The Court relied on Mange Ram v. Brij Mohan, which explained that Rule 1(3) allows the court to assist in procuring an unlisted witness, while Rule 1A permits a party to produce a witness without a summons.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding was a civil suit.
predicates.party_brought_witness_without_summons: A party brought a witness to give evidence without obtaining a court summons.
predicates.witness_was_omitted_from_list: The witness’s name was not included in the party’s list of witnesses.

issues.definition: In a civil suit, a party’s production of an unlisted witness without a summons does not, by itself, invalidate the witness’s examination.

issues.legal_issue: A sale of immovable property may pass title even if the whole purchase price has not been paid, provided the parties intended to transfer ownership and the price was paid or promised.
material_facts: The vendor executed and registered a sale deed conveying the property to the purchaser.
The deed recited a total price, part of which the purchaser allegedly had not paid.
The vendor admitted executing the deed and receiving the full consideration, and the deed and surrounding evidence showed an intention to transfer ownership.
issues.conclusion: The sale was not invalid merely because part of the purchase price might remain unpaid; title passed to the purchaser, subject to the vendor’s statutory charge for any unpaid purchase money.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act defines a sale as a transfer of ownership for a price paid, promised, or part-paid and part-promised; payment of the whole price at execution is not essential to completion of the sale. The intention to transfer ownership is assessed from the deed, conduct, and evidence. Section 55(4)(b) gives the seller a charge on the property for unpaid purchase money and interest. The Court referred to Gyatri Prasad v. Board of Revenue, Sukaloo v. Punau, Goode v. Burton, Webb v. Macpherson, Venkataperumal Naidu v. Rathnasabhapathi Chettiar, Shobhalal Shyamlal Kunni v. Sidhelal Halkelal Bania, and Basalingaya Revanshiddappa v. Chinnaya Karibasappa.

rule.if: civil_suit_involving_title_to_immovable_property and deed_was_executed_and_registered and parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership and price_was_paid_or_promised

predicates.civil_suit_involving_title_to_immovable_: The civil suit concerned title to immovable property.
predicates.deed_was_executed_and_registered: The parties executed and registered an instrument of transfer.
predicates.parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership: The parties intended the instrument to transfer ownership, rather than merely to create a future contract or a sham transaction.
predicates.price_was_paid_or_promised: The agreed price was paid, promised, or partly paid and partly promised.

issues.definition: When parties to a registered transfer of immovable property intend to transfer ownership for a paid or promised price, title passes despite unpaid purchase money, subject to the seller’s charge.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reverse concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal merely because the evidence might support another conclusion.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court concurrently found that the sale deed was genuine and conveyed title to the purchaser.
The High Court reversed those findings in a second appeal based on circumstances already considered by the lower courts.
The findings of the lower courts were based on evidence and were not shown to be perverse or such that no reasonable person could have reached them.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not legally entitled to set aside the concurrent findings of fact in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not permit interference with concurrent findings of fact unless the findings are perverse, based on no evidence, or such that no reasonable person could reach them on the evidence.

rule.if: second_appeal and lower_courts_made_concurrent_findings and findings_are_supported_by_evidence and findings_are_not_perverse

predicates.second_appeal: The matter was before the High Court in a second appeal.
predicates.lower_courts_made_concurrent_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_are_supported_by_evidence: Evidence in the record supports the lower courts’ factual finding.
predicates.findings_are_not_perverse: The finding is not one that no reasonable person could reach on the evidence.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, concurrent factual findings supported by evidence and not shown to be perverse must not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer subject to a repurchase condition in the same document is a mortgage by conditional sale when the parties intended the transfer as security, and refusal of a timely tender prevents the transaction from becoming an absolute sale for default.
material_facts: The document described the transaction as a mortgage by conditional sale and included in that same document a condition for repayment and reconveyance.
The contents of the document and the surrounding circumstances showed that the transfer was intended as security.
The mortgagor tendered repayment within the stipulated time, but the mortgagee refused to accept it.
The plaintiff held the property through a transfer from the mortgagor and sought redemption.
issues.conclusion: The transaction remained a mortgage by conditional sale because the mortgagor had tendered repayment and was not in default; the plaintiff as assignee was entitled to seek redemption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act requires the repurchase condition to be embodied in the document effecting or purporting to effect the sale. The controlling test is the parties’ intention, assessed from the document and surrounding circumstances; where the transfer is intended as security, it is a mortgage. The Court relied on Balkishen Das v. Legge, Bhaskar Woman Joshi v. Shrinarayan Rambilas Agarwal, and P.L. Bapuswami v. N. Pattay Gounder.

rule.if: redemption_suit and repurchase_condition_is_in_transfer_document and parties_intended_transfer_as_security and mortgagor_tendered_repayment and mortgagee_refused_tender

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding sought redemption of property held under a disputed transfer.
predicates.repurchase_condition_is_in_transfer_docu: The condition for repayment and reconveyance appears in the same document as the transfer.
predicates.parties_intended_transfer_as_security: The parties intended the transfer to secure repayment rather than to operate as an absolute sale.
predicates.mortgagor_tendered_repayment: The mortgagor offered repayment as required by the transaction.
predicates.mortgagee_refused_tender: The mortgagee refused to accept the repayment offered.

issues.definition: In a redemption suit, a transfer intended as security remains a mortgage where its document contains the repurchase condition and the mortgagee refuses the mortgagor’s tender of repayment, allowing an assignee to seek redemption.
